generation.hypothesis: Employing spark plasma sintering (SPS) with simultaneous pulsed electric current and moderate uniaxial pressure reduces the sintering temperature required for densification compared to conventional furnace sintering.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder-form precursors (e.g., high-entropy alloys or oxide ceramics) produced by conventional milling or mechanical alloying.
generation.intervention: Use a spark plasma sintering setup applying moderate pressure (e.g., 20–50 MPa) and rapid heating rates (on the order of hundreds of °C/min).
generation.conditions: Short dwell times (on the order of minutes) and inert/vacuum environment to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced mass transport facilitated by the applied electric current and localized heating at contact points between particles.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed current creates Joule heating and electroplastic effects at particle contacts, increasing diffusion and reducing the temperature needed for sintering.
generation.predicted_outcome: Achieve near-full densification at temperatures 200–300 °C lower than in conventional furnace sintering, with comparable or improved microstructural properties.
generation.baseline: Conventional furnace sintering at higher temperatures (e.g., 1200–1400 °C) and longer dwell times to drive densification.
generation.boundary: Highly refractory compositions or powders with large particle sizes may still require elevated temperatures or longer dwell times for complete densification.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of temperature reduction and final material properties may vary with powder composition, particle size, and SPS processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare densification and mechanical properties achieved by SPS and conventional furnace sintering for the same material and evaluate final microstructure using X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy.
measurements: Sintered density after identical dwell times
Extrinsic properties (e.g., hardness, strength) of the final product
Microstructural evolution (e.g., grain size, phase content) via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no improvement in sintering temperature or densification is observed via SPS compared to conventional sintering, or if final properties do not match or exceed those of conventionally sintered samples, the hypothesis is not supported.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . 2.1. Mechanical Alloying and Sintering

The Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr alloy (stoichiometric ratio) was prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The following elemental powders with commercial purity were used as feedstock: Al (99.9 wt.% purity, Sigma Aldrich, USA), Ti, Nb, V (over 99.5 wt.% purity, Alfa Aesar, Karlsruhe, Germany), Ta (99.9 wt.% purity, CRM, China) and Zr powder (99.5 wt.% purity, TLS Technik, Bitterfeld-Wolfen, Germany). The powders were handled before MA under argon in a high-purity atmosphere in a glovebox.

The precursor powders were mechanically alloyed in a Fritsch Pulverisette 6 planetary ball mill under different milling times to evaluate the evolution of their morphology and microstructure with the time of milling. The selected milling times were 0 (these were not milled, rather simply mixed together in a horizontal blender for 10 min for homogeneous blending), 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 h.
